conflict_topics: ventilation responsibility / who must ventilate when cooking
moving Agent C's drying rack / consent to move laundry
stove access / timing of stove release
dialogue_quality_notes: Speech is concise and context-dependent; participants give concrete time estimates (e.g., 'three minutes', '12 minutes').
Some repeated formulations: C repeats the plea not to move the drying rack twice with nearly identical wording.
Public environment updates keep the dialogue well-grounded in observable states (extractor on, window closed, who holds stove).
evaluation.final_reason: By the end of the transcript the immediate stove-access dispute was temporarily resolved by A releasing the stove, but the central substantive disagreements about who is responsible for ventilating, whether a standing rule should be imposed, and whether C's rack may be moved without consent remain unsettled. No round produced an affirmative, lasting settlement of these issues.
position_change_notes: Agent A softened immediate conflict by turning on the extractor and giving time estimates, and ultimately released the stove as promised (evidence: A turns on extractor, 'I'll release the stove in a minute', then physically releases it).

Agent B moved from an immediate demand for ventilation and a standing rule to accepting short timeframes ('Okay, three minutes'), showing tactical concession without abandoning the claim that cooks should ventilate.

Agent C consistently retained the position that their drying rack must not be moved without consent and explicitly offered to move the rack only if asked (Turn 10), maintaining a firm boundary while allowing a conditional accommodation.
Agent D assumed stove use (12 minutes) but did not state agreement to B's requested ventilation behaviors; D's position remains effectively unchanged and uncommitted on the ventilation/rack issue.

round_scores.evidence: A turns on the extractor and promises 5 minutes but had already refused B's demand to accept a standing ventilation rule; stove remains with A and C's laundry remains exposed by the closed window, so the substantive disagreement about who must ventilate and whether the rack may be moved remains active.

A asks for three more minutes and B accepts the three-minute timeframe and asks to be told when the stove is free; extractor remains on. The immediate timing dispute is narrowed, reducing escalation, but the underlying responsibility/rule and C's consent remain unsettled.

C explicitly intervenes: 'please don't move my drying rack or open the window. Ask me first; they're my work clothes.' This asserts a direct, incompatible demand with any proposal to open the rain-facing window and clarifies C's stake, increasing the substantive disagreement.

A physically releases the stove and leaves the extractor on; C thanks A and reiterates 'Please don't open the window or move my drying rack... If you need the window open, tell me and I'll move them.' The immediate stove-access friction is removed, and C offers a cooperative condition (they will move the rack if asked), but there is still no agreed rule about ventilation responsibility.

D takes the stove for 12 minutes (starts a new cooking period). B asks D to keep the extractor on and not to open/move C's rack without asking. D has not committed to those conditions; the issue is prolonged by another cook's session, keeping the substantive disagreement (ventilation responsibility vs. C's laundry exposure) active and potentially intensified by longer duration.

After 10 minutes from the start the confirmed state remains: window closed; extractor on; laundry exposed; stove with Agent D. No new agreement on a standing rule, no consent from C to unprompted movement of the rack, and no confirmed commitment from D beyond taking the stove, so substantive issues remain unresolved.

substantive_insights: No prior household rule creates uncertainty about who should bear the burden of odor control; participants appeal to different presumptive norms (cook's responsibility vs. asking a roommate to move belongings).
There is a practical trade-off between two ventilation options: extractor (low risk to C's laundry) versus opening the rain-facing window (which risks wetting C's work clothes).
C's explicit insistence on consent to move the drying rack creates a necessary condition for opening the window that the others must respect or find an alternative (e.g., extractor use).
Temporal commitments (A's short remaining cook time; D's 12-minute session) meaningfully affect how acute the conflict is, but do not resolve normative responsibility questions.
